doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Kundalini energy and Dizzy's divine playing
summary: Longo links music to base-of-spine energy and describes Dizzy's joy, unearthly playing and spiritual quality.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: And so there is a spiritual or a — you can call it metaphysical or whatever you want. A spiritual aspect of our music. Something that I mentioned in the DVD that I learned from Dizzy about kundalini energy. I don’t know if — is this possible to say —

There’s a movie called A Night in Havanna. And Lorraine got mad at Dizzy ‘cause this woman asked Dizzy, she said, “Where does your music come from?” He said, “You really want to know?” She said, “Yeah.” He said, “My asshole.” And everybody — © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

Lorraine got mad. But he was serious. Because the energy at the base of your spine man, if you look up the thing called kundalini energy, that’s a part of our music. Now if you notice, there’s a history of Beethoven grunting all the time. Oscar Peterson grunted. Erroll Gardner grunted. Because they’re coming from that base of the spine kind of — and that’s got to be in the music. If that’s not there you’re playing without a bottom to your music. Now that energy there is pretty much a metaphysical thing that causes the music to have a divine quality to it. And Dizzy was aware of the divinity. I think Sonny Rollins, he knew Dizzy was a celestial being. And I saw that. I saw that with Dizzy. He was the most amazing human being I ever met in my life, man. All those years I spent with him. I never met another person in my life like that. And some of the stuff he would play when I was playing behind him, I would say oh my — I would be — I remember in Florida once he and I went down and we were playing with some guys from down there. And we were playing “Stella by Starlight.” And I played a solo that was really hip. And Dizzy picked up his horn and he blew some stuff that made it sound like — I screamed. He was playing so — I don’t know where that was coming from. Unearthly. Coming from some other place.
Were you playing it as a ballad?
Were you playing it as a ballad?
Okay. I’m just trying to imagine what he would have played to make you scream.

Oh man he was playing stuff not even on the trumpet. I mean I don’t know where he was coming from but it caused me to scream it was so exciting what he played. I couldn’t believe it. I says holy — what the fuck is that? And that happened to me a lot when I was first with him because the first I played with him I was so inspired just playing with him that I played very well. He gave me a piece he had written for Japan and I sight read it. And Dizzy was saying, “Hell yes, hell yes.” The next night [scats] — I said, “What, you mean you’ve got to do this every night?” He said, “What the hell do you think I’m paying you for.” And so I said oh man, I’ve got some stuff to learn. Because he played on that level every single — look — see that picture up there?

That was Dizzy 24 hours a day. I never saw Dizzy ever depressed. Ever. He totally escaped neurosis. And we lived, like he would stay at my parents’ house, and often times I stayed with his relatives. And so I observed Dizzy waking up in the morning and then — he was like that all the time. I never saw him ever depressed. And I asked him once, “Man how do you do that?” He said, “I decided early on in life to become a creature of joy.” And I asked him once also, “What is your music about?” And he said, “Absolute © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

love for every man, woman, child, gay and lesbian on the planet.” And Dizzy had — if you ever listen to an album called “The Man From Monterey” he plays “The Shadow of Your Smile.” I couldn’t play it for two years after he died. It’s unexplainable beauty. And he only plays one chorus, the melody chorus. But it’s so gorgeous man, it’s like — what is this? It’s coming from some other place. And he had that. It’s divine. It’s like Sarah Vaughan. We used to call Sarah “the divine Miss Vaughan.” She has that in her music too. And so I guess some of it comes from the sanctifying church. The way I look at it as what religion calls the holy spirit. That’s what’s in the music. Now some people are just playing the notes, they’re not playing the holy spirit. They’re missing that part.
